title: The Claims Machine: Offices, Reports, and Proof
intro: How a claim travels from research desk to negotiating table, and what proof it must carry.

terms.def: The longest negotiation stage, settling the issues from the framework agreement into the shape of the final deal.
The independent 1991 body that holds public inquiries into comprehensive claims the federal government rejects.

body: After Calder, Ottawa built the machinery. The Office of Native Land Claims receives comprehensive files, Specific Claims West handles specific claims across the west including Alberta, and reviewers test the evidence. The 1985 Coolican Report, Living Treaties, Lasting Agreements, then indicted the whole federal approach for falling short of fairness and justice, and Ottawa answered with reforms shaped by its findings.

A comprehensive claim must prove five things: an organized society, occupation since time immemorial that was established fact when Europeans asserted sovereignty, occupation mostly excluding other societies, continued traditional use, and title never touched by treaty or other lawful means. Then INAC reviews the file for legal merit, provinces or territories join because the disputed lands sit inside their borders, and negotiation begins.

Rejection is not the end. Since 1991 a nation can ask the Indian Claims Commission to hold a public inquiry into a refused comprehensive claim, while its sibling body reviews specific-claim disputes, and both sometimes mediate. Only if review fails does the nation face the last resort, a lawsuit, with crippling costs, years of delay, and a winner-takes-all ending that breeds confrontation. The chapter is blunt: both sides prefer the table.

The machine moves slowly: in the first thirty years of claims policy, 1973 to 2003, only fifteen comprehensive claims reached resolution. The Algonquins of Golden Lake show one file mid-journey, with a claim territory map reaching past Algonquin Park toward Petawawa and objectives that name the pattern, identify and protect Algonquin rights while keeping the park a park for everyone.

example.title: Read a claim file
example.text: Open the Algonquins of Golden Lake map the way Lesson 5 will open Bigstone's: find the claim territory, the overlapping interests, and the affected communities. Those three layers are the anatomy every 2.2 profile must name.

check.prompt: Name two of the five tests a comprehensive claim must meet, and say where a rejected claim goes next.
check.sample: Sample response: occupation since time immemorial and title never touched by treaty, for example; a rejected comprehensive claim can go to the Indian Claims Commission for a public inquiry.

title: Specific Claims and the Bigstone Cree
intro: Broken promises, audited one by one, plus the urban reserve idea.

terms.def: A claim that the Crown failed to keep a treaty promise, such as a reserve that was never surveyed.
The northern Alberta nation whose specific claim over treaty-versus-scrip losses is the chapter's worked example.
Reserve land inside a city, such as the 1982 Opawikoscikan addition to the Peter Ballantyne Cree Nation, created to share economic opportunity.

body: Specific claims are audits of promises. Researchers reconstruct what the treaty said, what the Crown delivered, and where the two diverge, across reserve selection, annuities, implements, and schooling. Settlements stall on hard practical questions the chapter names outright: assessing the precise entitlement, choosing replacement lands, agreeing fair compensation, and untangling third-party interests already on the ground.

The Bigstone Cree Nation of northern Alberta is the worked file. When Treaty 8 commissioners offered a choice, community members split between taking treaty and taking scrip, 106 accepting scrip payments instead of treaty status, and extended-family groups carried the consequences for generations. Their claim map shows the anatomy to copy: the traditional territory and claim area, the overlapping industrial and community interests, and the affected Bigstone communities and reserves.

Fair settlements can also invent new ground. Since the early 1980s, Saskatchewan First Nations have bought city land and converted it into reserves through agreements with municipalities, beginning with the Opawikoscikan reserve that the Peter Ballantyne Cree Nation established in Prince Albert in 1982. Unlike reserves swallowed later by urban sprawl, these are deliberate city purchases, holding the same legal status as rural reserves, with municipal deals covering law enforcement, taxation, and services.

The chapter frames urban reserves as economic self-sufficiency feeding self-government: diverse income and jobs inside city limits. For Assignment 2.2, Bigstone is your template paragraph, events, issues, settlement or decision, and a timeline, and your second Alberta file should contrast it, ideally a comprehensive-style file so the two paragraphs compare roads as well as names.

example.title: Anatomy of a 2.2 paragraph
example.text: Paragraph on Bigstone: open with the treaty-or-scrip split, add the map's three layers as your issues, close with the claim's current status from the nation's own site. Repeat the skeleton for your second file and the contrast writes itself.

check.prompt: What makes Saskatchewan's urban reserves different from most others in Canada?
check.sample: Sample response: most urban reserves began as rural reserves later surrounded by sprawl or annexation, while Saskatchewan's were created by First Nations deliberately buying city land and converting it, starting with Opawikoscikan in 1982.

title: When Talks Fail: Paths to Resolution
intro: Cardston, Oka, and Lubicon, and the spectrum from negotiation to resistance.

terms.def: The 1990 seventy-eight-day armed standoff at Kanesatake over the Pines, ending years later in a land governance deal.
The northern Alberta nation that fought for its land rights through Olympic protests and an international timber boycott.

body: Centuries of waiting push some nations past the table. In July 1980, Kainai members blockaded an access road near Cardston, Alberta, with a large tipi, asking only that Ottawa negotiate their long-outstanding Big Claim, rooted in Elders' accounts of a 99-year Mormon lease that had expired. The RCMP answered with dogs on July 26, arrests followed, and the claim remains unsettled.

Canada's most famous confrontation came at Oka in 1990. The town wanted to clear the Pines for nine more golf holes; Kanesatake Haudenosaunee called the same ground sacred territory claimed for nearly 300 years, since a 1717 French grant made without consulting them, with federal rejections as recent as 1975 and 1986. After Oka walked out of talks and announced construction, residents barricaded the dirt road, provincial police stormed the barricade, an officer was shot dead, and a seventy-eight-day standoff drew in Kahnawake, the Mercier Bridge blockade, and finally the army. A land governance deal followed in December 2000.

The Lubicon Lake Cree chose pressure over barricades. At the 1988 Calgary Olympics their Chief Bernard Ominayak trailed the Petro-Canada torch relay with press releases about drilling on unceded Lubicon land, then supporters ran a 1991 to 1998 international boycott that stopped timber cutting on Lubicon territory until land rights settle. Alberta granted a reserve, but federal negotiations on the rest have dragged on since 2000.

The chapter arrays the methods on a spectrum, negotiation, lawsuits, blockades, media pressure, armed resistance, and asks which fits which case. Its checkpoint is blunt: define ceded land, non-ceded land, and both claim types with an example each, then name what blocks settlement. If Oka and Lubicon sit clearly on your spectrum, with Cardston beside them, you are ready for the peoples the treaty system skipped.

example.title: Place them on the spectrum
example.text: Cardston: peaceful blockade met with force, claim still open. Oka: barricade to standoff to a 2000 deal. Lubicon: media plus boycott, partial wins, talks ongoing. Three methods, three different prices and payoffs.

check.prompt: Why did the Oka dispute escalate from a municipal golf course to an armed standoff?
check.sample: Sample response: the Pines carried a nearly 300-year-old title dispute with recent federal rejections, talks collapsed when Oka announced construction, and the barricade, injunction, and deadly police raid pulled in Kahnawake and the army.
